title: The Rover That Fits: Width, Clearance and Replanning

questions.question: A grid planner returns the shortest route through a room with a 0.40 m gap straight ahead and a 1.50 m gap off to the side. Which does it take, and why?
options: The narrow one, because a search over cells plans for a point and a narrow gap is usually the direct way
The wide one, because A* prefers open space
Whichever has fewer cells to expand
It depends on the heuristic
questions.explanation: Measured: the point route was 6.900 m and cleared 0.200 m. The route for a 0.25 m robot was 8.060 m and cleared 0.316 m. The shortest route is shortest because it goes through the gap the robot does not fit through.

questions.question: Why grow the obstacles by the robot's radius rather than checking the robot's footprint at each step of the search?
options: It moves the geometry into the map once instead of into every step of the search for ever
It is more accurate
It allows diagonal movement
It is the only way to handle unknown cells
questions.explanation: It also gives the right answer when the robot fits nowhere: a radius of 0.50 m on that map returned no route at all, rather than a route it could not drive.

questions.question: The inflation uses a disc rather than a square, and rounds the radius up to whole cells. What do those two choices do?
options: The disc avoids over-blocking diagonals by root two and closing gaps the robot fits through; rounding up keeps the map from claiming the robot fits when it does not
Both are performance optimisations
The disc is more conservative and rounding up is less so
Neither matters at a 10 cm resolution
questions.explanation: Rounding up makes inflation conservative by up to one cell, which belongs in the margin rather than being a surprise. Unknown also grows as unknown rather than as occupied, since a cell beside unseen ground is not known to be blocked.

questions.question: A route planned with a 0.25 m inflation clears 0.316 m at its tightest. The robot drives it with a 1 m lookahead and a pose 100 ms old. How close does the robot get?
options: 0.068 m: the follower's corner cut comes out of the same margin the inflation provided
0.316 m, since it is following the route
About 0.25 m, its own radius
More than 0.316 m, since the follower smooths the route
questions.explanation: At a 0.30 m lookahead it cleared 0.337 and at 0.60 it cleared 0.255. How much the robot clears is decided by the follower, not by the plan.

questions.question: What should the inflation radius actually be set from?
options: The robot's radius plus about 0.27 of the lookahead plus speed times the estimator's latency plus half a cell
The robot's radius, which is what inflation is for
The robot's radius doubled, as a safety factor
Whatever leaves a route through the narrowest gap
questions.explanation: Every term is measurable and three were measured in earlier lessons. It runs the other way too: shortening the lookahead or reducing the estimator's latency buys clearance directly, so a robot that cannot fit down an aisle at speed may fit down it slowly.

questions.question: A pallet is put down on the route after it was planned. The map is updated correctly. Why does the robot still drive into it?
options: A plan is a photograph of a map and holds no reference to it, so nothing asked the question again
The map update was too slow
The follower ignores the map
The pallet was marked unknown rather than occupied
questions.explanation: Checking the remaining route against the inflated map is a walk down a few hundred cells against a search that expands tens of thousands, which is what makes checking affordable every tick and replanning only on demand.
